subject: How to constrain the inverse logit of a parametre

messages.author: 83b63066408210ec
messages.subject: How to constrain the inverse logit of a parametre
parts:
I asked this question on Cross Validated for the formatting but I'll reproduce it here sans formatting:

There are four mutually exclusive events I want to model - or rather, three events and their absence. The three events' rate of occurrence together is very small, with a 99% chance none of them will occur. So I would model them with a multinomial. So far so good.

However, I know that the rate of occurrence of the ith event is given by Ti = inv.logit (Ai + Bi), where Ai can take any real value and Bi is nonnegative, and I have priors on these Ai and Bi, which are the quantities I am actually interested in modelling. Therefore, the parametres of the multinomial are transformed parametres.

But for the sampling to work, I need to constrain the Ai and Bi somehow, so as to make T1 + T2 + T3 < 1. Just constraining the transformed parametres doesn't seem to work, and it fails to sample. Is there a way to do it? I tried constraining the Ai to <= -2 but that is rather ad hoc and not the true constraint, and will not always work.

messages.author: 83b63066408210ec
messages.subject: Re: How to constrain the inverse logit of a parametre
parts: For clarification, I'm actually modelling the Ti over time and fitting them to a decreasing function, and Ai + Bi is the value Ti takes at t=0, so the problem isn't as underspecified as it looks. I just need to figure out how to constrain the parametres, the other things are (for now) taken care of.

messages.author: b1e64236b865525c
messages.subject: Re: How to constrain the inverse logit of a parametre
parts:
Just to make sure I understand your problem:
  • you're already using a simplex variable
  • for each individual probability, you have a functional form (or rather a functional form for the log-odds) and
  • since you're using the parameters of that function as your actual parameters (on which you have priors), you don't know how to impose constraints (more specifically, sum = 1) on your top-level stuff (the probabilities) because they're modeled as transformed parameters
I don't have an answer for that, but if it's true that the sum of all relevant probabilities is always very small (< 1%), you probably can estimate them as if they were independent (they're not, of course), using Beta distributions instead of the more general Dirichlet. To get an intuition on why that approximation works relatively well, try running the following chunk on R:

set.seed (19)
x = rdirichlet (1E5, c (1, 3, 96))
cor (x [, 1], x [, 2]) # - 0.0106
x = rdirichlet (1E5, c (20, 30, 50))
cor (x [, 1], x [, 2]) # - 0.3297
[meaning: the correlation between the estimates of very small components of Dirichlet distributions tends to be very small, and that's obviously not true about relatively large components]

That said, it would be nice if someone had a more rigorous and more general answer.

I would go with

parameters {
  simplex[3] T_raw; // sums to 1
  real<lower=0,upper=1> scale;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[3] T = T_raw * scale; // sums to less than 1
}

and then make your prior on T_raw be Dirichlet with i-th shape parameter Ai + Bi or something.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to constrain the inverse logit of a parametre
parts:
I think Ben's way of doing things is probably going to
be more reasonable. Usually hard constraints on things
are a bad idea.

If you have parameters

vector[3] A;
vector<lower=0>[3] B;

and a transformed parameter:

vector[3] T = inv_logit(A + B);

then in order to make

sum(T) < 1,

you have to control A and B, which is tricky.

Yu can do it with just 3 by brute force by constraining
each variable in turn. Let me show you how to start:

The first constraint is automatically satisfied:

inv_logit(A[1] + B[1]) < 1

But now we need

inv_logit(A[2] + B[2]) < 1 - inv_logit(A[1] + B[1])

You can solve for the necessary constraint on A[2].

A[2] < logit(1 - inv_logit(A[1] + B[1])) - B[2]

So A[1], B[1] and B[2] can be unconstrained, but
we have the above upper-bound on A[2]. Similarly
B[3] can be unconstrained, and then you'll find another
upper bound on A[3] the same way.

Not pretty, but there's no other way to do it.

- Bob

> On Thursday, 9 February 2017 03:56:22 UTC-2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I think Ben's way of doing things is probably going to
> be more reasonable.  Usually hard constraints on things
> are a bad idea.
>
> If you have parameters
>
> vector[3] A;
> vector<lower=0>[3] B;
>
> and a transformed parameter:
>
> vector[3] T = inv_logit(A + B);
>
> then in order to make
>
>   sum(T) < 1,
>
> you have to control A and B, which is tricky.  
>
> Yu can do it with just 3 by brute force by constraining
> each variable in turn.  Let me show you how to start:
>
> The first constraint is automatically satisfied:
>
>   inv_logit(A[1] + B[1]) < 1
>
> But now we need
>
>   inv_logit(A[2] + B[2]) < 1 - inv_logit(A[1] + B[1])
>
> You can solve for the necessary constraint on A[2].  
>
>   A[2] < logit(1 - inv_logit(A[1] + B[1])) - B[2]
>
> So A[1], B[1] and B[2] can be unconstrained, but
> we have the above upper-bound on A[2].  Similarly
> B[3] can be unconstrained, and then you'll find another
> upper bound on A[3] the same way.
>
> Not pretty, but there's no other way to do it.
>
> - Bob
